newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Saudi prince touted as Fokker saviour.
newsitem.headline: Saudi prince touted as Fokker saviour.

text.p: A billionaire Saudi prince with global financial interests is the latest potential saviour for Dutch plane maker Fokker which, though bankrupt for over a year, refuses to be consigned to corporate history.
A string of suitors for the once proud aircraft pioneer -- from Canadians to Koreans and Russians -- has come and gone, with constant rumours of fresh interest.
There is currently one confirmed interested party -- the Malaysian state.
But this week Saudi Arabian Prince al-Waleed bin Talal, mega-rich nephew of King Fahd, has been touted as a possible white knight.

Dutch media said this week that the 39-year old prince, with stakes in Paris's Euro Disney and London's Canary Warf, sent a fax via a third party to the Dutch government, still a minority Fokker shareholder, expressing interest in relaunching the Fokker marque.
A government spokesman, however, denied that the prince, whose latest acquisition is the presitgious George V hotel in Paris, had been in touch with the government.
"We have had no contact with him," he said, adding that contact had possibly been with Fokker's receivers.
"The only people talking at the moment are the Dutch and Malaysian governments, Fokker receivers and Stork," a spokesman for the economic affairs ministry in The Hague said.

After Fokker was cut loose by Germany's Daimler-Benz last March, Dutch engineer Stork bought up the profitable aircraft maintenance and components businesses in a deal binding it to some involvement in a relaunch.
On Wednesday, Stork chairman Jan Hovers denied that Stork was blocking a Fokker rebirth and said talks were continuing, involving his company.
"Stork has always been a constructive party (in the Fokker talks), also because as a supplier we have an economic interest in a sound restart," he said.
Fokker's receivers declined any comment to the media.
It was unclear why the prince could be interested in what is left of Fokker and what he would do with it if he bought it.

The prince, who heads United Saudi Commerical Bank and holds substantial stakes in Citicorp, U.S. retail group Saks Fifth Avenue, the Plaza Hotel in New York and the Four Seasons and Fairmont hotel chains, last year teamed up with pop superstar Michael Jackson to cooperate on concerts, films, television, theme parks and hotels.
A more realistic Fokker rescue appears to rest with talks between the Dutch and Malaysian government, but a deal looks increasingly unlikely.
With Fokker's factory near Amsterdam finishing a handful of outstanding orders, most of its skilled labour force has long since left.
Industry sources say any relaunch would face massive start-up costs and could take up to a year to get into business.
The government spokesman said the Malaysian proposal involved taking a 49 percent stake in a new entity in a deal which would keep production units in the Netherlands.
"Who would own the rest of the company has not been decided -- that's what's being talked about now," he said.
But time is running out.
Unless a deal can be reached, the Fokker plant will shut down in the summer and remaining assets liquidated.
